queue.label: protect-the-downside
queue.content:
The habit that has served me best across two very different industries: decide what the worst realistic outcome is, make sure you survive it, and only then get interested in the upside.

It sounds unambitious. It's the opposite. Surviving your bad years is what lets you still be in the room for the good ones.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/protect-the-downside.html

queue.label: culture-of-ownership
queue.content:
You can't ask people to act like owners while reserving every real decision for yourself. They notice.

Ownership isn't a value you post on a wall. It's a series of moments where someone made a call you would have made differently, and you let it stand.

Most cultures die in those moments.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/culture-of-ownership.html

queue.label: beverage-distribution
queue.content:
New beverage founders think the hard part is getting a distributor. The hard part starts after.

A distributor gives you access, not effort. Your brand is one of hundreds in their book, and attention follows velocity - which you have to create yourself, store by store.

Signing the agreement is the beginning of the work, not the end of it.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/beverage-distribution.html

queue.label: hiring-in-the-age-of-ai-provieo
queue.content:
AI didn't break hiring by making candidates worse. It broke hiring by making every application look equally good.

When the signal disappears from the document, employers fall back on networks and pedigree - which is a worse world, not a better one.

The way out is evidence: real work, with the reasoning visible.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/hiring-in-the-age-of-ai-provieo.html

queue.label: the-long-game-patience
queue.content:
Most of what compounds in a business is invisible for years. Reputation, bench strength, the habit of doing the unglamorous thing properly.

None of it shows up in a quarter. All of it shows up in a decade.

The hardest discipline in operating isn't working harder. It's being willing to wait for the return.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-long-game-patience.html

queue.label: engineering-the-energy-curve
queue.content:
Most energy products are engineered for the first twenty minutes. That's why the crash is the category's defining experience.

The interesting problem isn't peak intensity - it's the shape of the curve. Onset, plateau, and how gracefully it comes down.

Formulate for how someone feels at hour three, not at minute five.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/engineering-the-energy-curve.html

queue.label: finance-discipline-startups
queue.content:
Financial discipline in a young company isn't about spending less. It's about knowing, at any moment, which number would actually kill you.

Most founders can recite revenue. Fewer can tell you their true landed cost, and fewer still can tell you when the cash runs out under a realistic case.

Know the one that kills you.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/finance-discipline-startups.html

queue.label: provieo-both-sides-of-the-hire
queue.content:
I've spent years on the employer side of hiring, and I built Provieo from the candidate side. The strange part is how similar the complaint is.

Employers say they can't tell who can actually do the work. Candidates say they can't show it. Same broken channel, two directions.

Fix the channel and both problems get smaller.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/provieo-both-sides-of-the-hire.html

queue.label: functional-beverage-market
queue.content:
The functional beverage market keeps getting described as crowded. It isn't crowded - it's undifferentiated, which is a different problem with a different fix.

Dozens of brands are chasing the same broad wellness consumer with the same hero ingredients at the same underdosed levels.

There's enormous room for anyone willing to own one occasion and actually deliver on it.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/functional-beverage-market.html

queue.label: learning-by-building-provieo-method
queue.content:
You don't learn judgment from a course. You learn it from making a decision, living with the result, and having to explain it to someone.

That's the loop AI is quietly removing from early-career work, and it's the loop we designed Provieo around rebuilding.

Build something real, then defend the choices. That's the whole method.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/learning-by-building-provieo-method.html

queue.label: introducing-provieo
queue.content:
I started Provieo because of a pattern I kept seeing from the hiring side: capable people who couldn't prove it, screened out by a document that measures the wrong thing.

The premise is simple. Stop claiming skills. Show the work, and show the thinking behind it.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/introducing-provieo.html

queue.label: the-headcount-trap
queue.content:
There is a particular relief that comes from deciding to hire. The team is stretched, something is slipping, and adding a person feels like decisive action.

I have felt that relief many times and I have learned to distrust it. A role you add under pressure gets defined by the pressure, so the job description becomes a list of everything currently on fire.

More often than I would like to admit, the headcount did not fix the problem. It gave the problem a person to hide behind.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-headcount-trap.html

queue.label: winning-the-cooler-door
queue.content:
Founders love to talk about distribution. Getting the can into the store is a real milestone, and we have earned plenty of them.

But distribution and merchandising are two different games. A distribution win is a purchase order. A merchandising win is a can a real person actually pulls off the shelf.

You can be authorized in a thousand stores and still lose at the cooler door, in the three seconds a shopper is standing there.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/winning-the-cooler-door.html

queue.label: the-reference-check-is-broken
queue.content:
By the time most of us pick up the phone for a reference check, we have already decided. The candidate handed us the names, and the names were chosen because they will say something kind.

If a step in your hiring process cannot change your mind, it is not a check. It is a formality.

What finally moved me was noticing how often a warm reference call preceded a hire that did not work, and how rarely the call had warned me.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-reference-check-is-broken.html

queue.label: hiring-for-judgment
queue.content:
For a long time the bottleneck in most work was production. The people who could draft, model and build quickly were valuable because that competence was scarce.

That world is ending. When anyone with good tools can produce a competent draft in minutes, output stops separating candidates.

What is left is deciding what to build, when it is right, and when to throw it out and start over. Judgment is the thing I screen for now.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/hiring-for-judgment.html

queue.label: cash-conversion-cycle
queue.content:
Founders love to talk about revenue. In a physical-product business I watch a quieter number first: the cash conversion cycle.

It measures how long a dollar is trapped between paying for cans, syrup, co-packing and freight, and the day a customer's payment actually lands.

Software collects before it spends. Beverage does the opposite. That one metric explains more about who survives than most of the income statement.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/cash-conversion-cycle.html

queue.label: the-apprenticeship-gap
queue.content:
A recent hire told me her worry was not that AI would take her job someday. It was that it had already taken the job she was supposed to have first.

Cleaning up the deck, reconciling the numbers, drafting the memo nobody read closely - a model does that in seconds now.

But that work was never really about the output. It was how people learned the shape of a business. We have not been honest about what its disappearance costs.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-apprenticeship-gap.html

queue.label: pricing-a-functional-drink
queue.content:
New founders treat price as the last decision, something you back into once the formula and the can are done. I think it is one of the first.

The number printed on the can is one of the loudest things a brand says about itself. Sit a dollar under the category leader and you have told the shopper exactly what you think you are worth.

Costs plus a margin gets the arithmetic right and the strategy backwards.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/pricing-a-functional-drink.html

queue.label: proof-over-pedigree
queue.content:
For most of my career I hired the way almost everyone does: read the resume, scan the schools and company names, form a quick impression.

Over time I noticed how often that impression was wrong in both directions. Impressive resumes hid people who could not deliver, and some of my best hires looked unremarkable on paper.

A resume tells you where someone has been, not what they can do today. That gap is why I built Provieo.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/proof-over-pedigree.html

queue.label: the-first-ninety-days
queue.content:
You can tell a great deal about a company by what happens to someone in their first ninety days. Not the welcome lunch - whether the work they were hired to do actually arrives.

I have broken that promise before without meaning to. You hire someone in a burst of conviction, the fire that made you hire them moves on, and they spend a month waiting.

Onboarding is where a company either keeps the promises it made to get someone in the door, or quietly hopes the new hire is too polite to mention it.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-first-ninety-days.html

queue.label: why-functional-drinks-fail-year-two
queue.content:
Launching a functional beverage has never been easier. Formulate quickly, find a co-packer, design a premium can, buy enough attention to reach a few thousand hands.

Year one can look like success. Year two is when most of these brands quietly disappear, and it is rarely the product's fault.

A launch measures your ability to generate trial. The business is the second purchase, and the tenth. Trial can be bought. Loyalty has to be earned.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/why-functional-drinks-fail-year-two.html

queue.label: portfolio-is-the-new-resume
queue.content:
The resume had a good run. For a century it was a cheap, loose proxy for what someone could do.

That correlation is breaking fast. A document anyone can now generate to look perfect carries no information - when every applicant passes, it decides nothing.

When claims are free, proof becomes the scarce thing. Show the work.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/portfolio-is-the-new-resume.html

queue.label: the-discipline-of-no
queue.content:
Early on I assumed the hard part of building a business was finding opportunities. Twenty-five years later I believe the opposite.

Opportunities are everywhere. A new channel, a promising co-packer, a flavor extension a retailer swears will sell - each arrives wearing the costume of progress.

Resources are finite, so every yes is a quiet no somewhere else. Choosing what to walk away from is the discipline that actually compounds.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-discipline-of-no.html

queue.label: hire-slow-first-ten
queue.content:
My most expensive mistakes in business were not bad deals or missed markets. They were hiring the wrong person too early.

When a company is small there is no layer of process to absorb a weak hire. Each person is a large fraction of the whole, writing the rulebook by example.

The pace they keep becomes the company's pace. The quality they accept becomes its floor. The first ten decide what the company becomes long before strategy does.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/hire-slow-first-ten.html

queue.label: what-ai-changes-about-starting-a-career
queue.content:
A lot of people starting out are anxious that AI has erased the bottom rung of the ladder. I understand the worry, but I think it misreads the change.

AI does the mechanical first pass faster than any junior person can. What it cannot do is decide which analysis matters, or notice when an answer is confidently wrong.

The first rung has not been removed. It has moved, and it now sits higher than it used to.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/what-ai-changes-about-starting-a-career.html

queue.label: trust-is-the-real-product
queue.content:
Walk the cooler aisle and the formulas blur together. The claims rhyme. Focus, energy, calm, all promising roughly the same thing.

Formulation is rarely the moat. Contract manufacturers are excellent, good ingredients are available to everyone, and a competitor can approximate your recipe within a season.

The real product is a promise someone is willing to believe a second time.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/trust-is-the-real-product.html

queue.label: reinvention-mid-career
queue.content:
Changing careers in your forties or fifties is supposed to be reckless. I have done it more than once - finance to beverages, then to building an AI company.

The fear assumes you are starting from zero. You are not. Decades in one field leave you with judgment, pattern recognition, a network, and the ability to read a situation fast.

The best reinventions are not leaps. They are transfers.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/reinvention-mid-career.html

queue.label: nootropics-substance-vs-hype
queue.content:
Nootropic has become one of the most overused words on a beverage label, and increasingly it is applied to products that have not earned it.

The category is not snake oil and it is not magic. Some ingredients have real evidence behind them at real doses, and plenty are there to look good on a panel.

Consumers deserve a clearer way to tell the difference than the front of the can.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/nootropics-substance-vs-hype.html

queue.label: breaking-the-experience-paradox
queue.content:
You cannot get the job without experience, and you cannot get the experience without the job. The longer you look at that, the more absurd it gets.

When talented people cannot break in they tend to blame themselves - not enough hustle, wrong school, bad luck. The barrier is structural, not personal.

Employers de-risk hiring by asking for proof, and the only sanctioned proof has been a prior job. That is the specific problem I built Provieo to solve.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/breaking-the-experience-paradox.html
